The overall strategy is correct: since \(P\) has degree \(5\) and vanishes at each \(r_j^2\), it must be a nonzero constant multiple of \(\prod (z-r_j^2)\). Evaluating the resulting products via \(Q(1),Q(-1),Q(i),Q(-i)\) is efficient and leads to the correct answer
\[
-\frac{2010012}{2010013}.
\]

However, there is a typographical/sign issue in the long intermediate product manipulation involving the factors at \(i\) and \(-i\); as written, that line does not cleanly match the subsequent conclusion. It would be clearer to state directly that
\[
\prod_j(1-r_j^2)=Q(1)Q(-1)
\]
and
\[
\prod_j(1+r_j^2)=-Q(i)Q(-i),
\]
which immediately gives
\[
\frac{P(1)}{P(-1)}=\frac{Q(1)Q(-1)}{Q(i)Q(-i)}.
\]
This avoids the confusing sign bookkeeping.
